newsitem.title: UK: Gold market sweats over IMF gold sale plan.
newsitem.headline: Gold market sweats over IMF gold sale plan.

text.p: Gold prices dipped lower on Thursday as market jitters mounted over the International Monetary Fund's plan to sell part of its gold reserves to help poor countries.
"It's very psychological. Everyone knows it's not much gold spread over a long time and there's no guarantee it will even happen," a London-based dealer said.
"But it's still making the market very nervous."
Gold fixed at a fresh two-month low of $382.20 an ounce in the morning, down $1.30 from Wednesday afternoon's fix. Dealers said it was vulnerable to erode further to $380 an ounce.
Prices have been sliding amid bearish market sentiment for days, ignoring potentially bullish news such has indication of strong U.S. economic growth and U.S.-Iraq tension.
An IMF meeting to discuss ways to finance loans and debt relief to poor countries, slated for Friday, has heightened nervousness.
IMF leadership has proposed selling five million of the Fund's 104 million ounces of gold to help pay for the aid, backed by most member nations including the U.S. and Britain.

Fuelling speculation were comments late on Wednesday by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, who said the IMF was very close to an agreement to sell some gold. A few member nations, including Germany, have opposed the plan.
But gold market analysts say the sales, if approved, would be small enough to be easily absorbed and structured over time to avoid disrupting the market.
"The market has just talked itself into despair and I think it's overdone," said analyst Rhona O'Connell of T. Hoare and Co.
"As far as the fundamental logistics are concerned, it's 30 tonnes a year over five years which should in principle make no difference," O'Connell added.
In the 1970s, the IMF sold about 25 million ounces of gold with little impact on the market, analysts said. About 3,500 tonnes of gold are consumed annually.
Nevertheless, U.S. investment funds have taken advantage of the market's shaky technical indicators and anxiety over the IMF sales to push down the price, analysts said.
The other precious metals, which often take cues from movements in the gold price, were also on shaky ground.
Platinum shed more than $3 overnight and fixed at a two-month low of $390 an ounce, despite the seasonal lull approaching an end.
Platinum's slide was linked to weakness in its sister metal palladium, which tumbled to close to three-year lows on Wednesday, dealers said.
Palladium, a rare white metal used in the auto and electronics industry, was trading slightly below Wednesday's levels at $122.00 an ounce.
Silver traded just three cents lower at $5.08 an ounce, but dealers said it was vulnerable to tumbling below the key $5.00 an ounce level in the absence of buying interest.
